title: Sikh thought close
hookLine: God, the self, ethics and the world, through the Guru's eyes

lines: WHICH IDEA CAME HOME WITH YOU?
cards: Some of what we learn slips away by the end of the week. Some ideas don't. They lodge somewhere, like a pebble in a shoe, and you keep noticing them at odd moments: in traffic, at the sink, halfway through an argument.
This stretch of the path has been about Sikh thought: what the Gurus taught about God, about the self, about how to live, and about the world we share. Today it closes. Not with a test.
With a walk back through the rooms, and a question at the end: which idea came home with you?

teach.h: GOD: ONE, NAMED IN MANY WAYS.
teach.b: First, God. The Granth opens with Ik Onkar, the One, and you met the names: Waheguru, the Wonderful Lord, and many others drawn from many tongues.
You met God with qualities and without, vast and close, beyond everything and within everyone. Second, the self. Haumai, ego, which isn't the same as you.
The mind as a friend to be trained, not an enemy to be beaten. Hukam, the order, and effort inside it. Grace and deeds.

teach.h: THE SELF: EGO, MIND, FREE WHILE LIVING.
teach.b: This life as the chance, and the hope of being free while still living. Third, how to live. The thieves that clutch and crave: attachment, greed, desire out of place.

teach.h: LIVING: THIEVES, RISING SPIRITS, THE GURMUKH.
teach.b: Against them, chardi kala, rising spirits, and bhaana, accepting the will. Ardas that asks and then accepts. The portrait of the Gurmukh, humble and truthful and serving, and of the Khalsa.

teach.h: THE WORLD: EQUAL SOULS, AN OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: Equal souls. Women as equals. Force only as the last resort, justice for the wronged, truth spoken to rulers.
Then the week just gone: many tongues in one script, the Word that is sung, kesh as given, the langar row, the open door, honest citizens, old words meeting new questions.
Underneath it all sits the question Guru Nanak asks in the first pauri of the Japji. In paraphrase: how do we become truthful, and how does the wall of falsehood come down?
His answer: by walking in the hukam, the order written with us. Much of this stretch can be heard as unpacking that line.

how: Sikhs study Gurmat, the Guru's teaching, through the Guru Granth Sahib, katha (talks explaining the hymns) in the gurdwara, and daily prayers such as the Japji, whose first pauri asks how to become truthful.

o: the Guru's view of God, self, life and world
the last exam that ends a course of study
a closing prayer said when the gurdwara shuts

games.q: Sikh thought close: tap the pairs.
p: ego, which isn't the same as you

s: in Sikh teaching, the mind is an enemy to be beaten
the mind is a friend to be trained.
the Japji's first pauri asks how the wall of falsehood comes down
Guru Nanak's answer: by walking in the hukam.
Sikh thought keeps God and daily life in separate rooms
the same teaching reaches the langar row, the open door and the tax form.

games.q: in the first pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak asks how we become truthful, and how the wall of falsehood comes down. which answer does he give?
o: by walking in the hukam, the divine order.
games.why: he sets aside outer cleansing, silence, piling up goods and cleverness, and answers: walk in the hukam, the order written with you.

practice: Let the rooms go by slowly: God, the self, how to live, the world. Don't pick the idea you think you should; wait for the one that has quietly been showing up in your days, the pebble in the shoe, and give it a name in a few words.
If you pray, offer thanks for it; if you don't, just hold it, and let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Sikh thought close. God, the self, how to live and the world, through the Guru's eyes, gathered under one question: how does the wall of falsehood come down? Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gurmat, the Guru's teaching, the Sikh way of thought.

carryVoice: Your line: the idea that stayed. A pebble in the shoe, carried home. A stretch of Sikh thought, closed.

sources.ref: Ang 1 (Japji, pauri 1: kiv sachiara hoiai kiv koorai tutai pal)
